newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Ciena seeks to add customers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Ciena seeks to add customers.

text.p: Ciena Corp, basking in the success of its February initial public offering, is gearing up to expand its customer base and add products to its roster, President and Chief Executive Patrick Nettles said on Friday.

"Our objectives this year clearly are to broaden the customer base ... while continuing to focus on delivering good customer service to existing customers," Nettles told Reuters in an interview a few days after the end of the company's "quiet period."

Nettles said the company had begun expanding its manufacturing capacity and was working on the development of new products, including the MultiWave 4000, a higher-capacity version of its current MultiWave 1600 product.

The MultiWave 1600 is a dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) system for long-distance fiberoptic telecommunications networks. It increases the carrying capacity of a single optical fiber 16 times by allowing simultaneous transmission of up to 16 optical channels per fiber.
By allowing more data to be transmitted over a fiber optic network, the system eases traffic congestion without requiring the installation of new fiber.

The MultiWave 4000 will have 40 channels, and "it takes the total capacity up to as much as 100 gigabits per second," Nettles said. The current 1600 system allows a fiber to carry signals at transmission speeds of up to 40 gigabits per second.
Nettles declined to set a release date for the new system. "It's basically driven by customer requirements," he said.

Ciena presently has three interexchange carriers (IXCs) as customers for its MultiWave 1600 product: U.S.-based Sprint Corp and WorldCom Inc, and a Japanese long-distance carrier called Teleway Japan Corp.

Nettles said the company would first focus on other domestic interexchange carriers in its efforts to expand the customer base. Beyond that, he said, Ciena was eyeing regional Bell operating companies as prospective customers as they entered the long-distance market. The company will also seek growth outside the United States, he said.
According to Chairman Jon Bayless, who also spoke to Reuters, the company was developing a separate product, with different technical requirements, to supply Bell operating companies.

Bayless is also general partner at Sevin Rosen Funds, the venture capital firm that backed Ciena. Sevin Rosen-led investments include such illustrious corporate names as Compaq Computer Corp, Lotus Development and Cyrix Corp.
"This is the best of all," Bayless said, referring to the Ciena investment.

Ciena went public on February 7 at $23 a share. The company ended its first day of trading with a market capitalization of about $3.7 billion, giving it the largest valuation of a venture-backed start-up in history, according to Sevin Rosen.
"In terms of growth potential, I think it has the same potential as Compaq. It can be a very large company," Bayless said.
When questioned during the interview, both Nettles and financial chief Joseph Chinnici declined to comment on either earnings projections or growth targets.

Montgomery Securities research analyst Michael Gordon, who initiated coverage of Ciena with a buy rating, said that he was estimating fiscal year 1997 earnings per share of $0.66 on revenues of $269 million, and 1998 EPS of $0.85 on revenues of $385 million.
The company had revenues of $54.8 million and earnings per share of $0.15 in its 1996 fiscal year, ended in October.
Gordon has forecast that the U.S. long-distance wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) market will grow to $2.5 billion in the next three to four years.
While any market of that size was going to attract competitors, Ciena had a substantial lead time over any rival.

The company also has the advantage of providing "open architecture characterized by very strong software capabilities," Gordon said. "They have the densest -- meaning the most number of waves or channels -- WDM systems commercially shipping."

Ciena already faces plenty of competition, and from companies with greater resources. Lucent Technologies Inc, Alcatel Alsthom Group, Northern Telecom Ltd, NEC Corp, Pirelli SpA, Siemens AG and ECI Telecom Ltd all offer various forms of transmission-enhancing equipment, according to Ciena's prospectus. Some, such as Lucent, already offer WDM equipment.
And the industry lends itself to intellectual property battles, as Ciena notes in its prospectus. In fact, a U.S. affiliate of Pirelli filed a suit against Ciena alleging patent infringement.
"We're vigorosly contesting," Nettles told Reuters. "We do not believe that we have infringed any valid patents."
((--Kamalakshi Mehta, New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610))
